content: Vaccine-mediated polio infection is also referred to by several terms, including vaccine-derived paralytic polio, vaccine-derived polio, paralytic polio due to vaccination, vaccine-related polio infection, and vaccine-associated polio. Overview The oral polio vaccine (OPV) is considered one of the safest and most effective vaccines available. It has successfully prevented millions of cases of polio, not only through direct immunization but also by establishing herd immunity within communities. However, in rare instances, the vaccine has been associated with cases of paralytic polio. There are two distinct subtypes of paralytic polio linked to OPV: vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP) and vaccine-derived paralytic polio (VDPP). Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP) Vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP) occurs when the attenuated strain of the poliovirus used in the vaccine undergoes genetic reversion within the intestine, transforming into a more virulent form. This virulent form can cause disease, but only in the vaccinated individual or in close, susceptible contacts. Importantly, VAPP does not lead to outbreaks. In developed countries, the risk of VAPP is highest following the administration of the first dose of the vaccine. Conversely, in developing countries, the risk increases with subsequent doses of the vaccine. Vaccine-Derived Paralytic Polio (VDPP) Vaccine-derived paralytic polio (VDPP) arises from a rare mutation in the original poliovirus strain contained in the vaccine. Unlike VAPP, VDPP has the potential to cause disease in any individual who is not immune to polio. Consequently, it can lead to outbreaks or even epidemics, particularly in communities lacking routine vaccination programs. When VDPP results in outbreaks, it is referred to as circulating vaccine-derived paralytic polio (cVDPP). Over the past decade, 24 reported outbreaks of VDPP have occurred, resulting in 750 cases of paralytic polio. Management of VDPP The management of VDPP involves implementing extensive vaccination campaigns in affected communities. The primary goal is to vaccinate every child in the area to halt the spread of the infection and prevent further cases.
